title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — Work, Energy and Power

summary: In the absence of non-conservative forces like friction, the total mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) of a system stays constant, even as it converts between the two forms.
explanation: As an object moves under a conservative force (like gravity), energy continuously converts between kinetic and potential forms, but the sum stays fixed. A ball dropped from height loses potential energy exactly as fast as it gains kinetic energy. When non-conservative forces (friction, air resistance) act, mechanical energy is no longer conserved on its own — some is converted to heat/sound — but the broader principle, total energy conservation across all forms, always holds.
commonMisconceptions: Applying 'conservation of mechanical energy' in situations with significant friction or air resistance without accounting for the energy lost to those forces.
Confusing 'conservation of mechanical energy' (a special case) with the universal 'conservation of energy' (which always holds, but may require tracking heat, sound, etc.).
examples: A pendulum swinging (ignoring air resistance): at the highest points, all energy is potential; at the lowest point, all energy is kinetic; the total stays constant throughout the swing.
genZNote: Energy doesn't disappear, it just changes outfits — potential to kinetic and back, unless friction steals some for itself.
